characters.name: Sana
characters.origin_detail: the ancient stone alleys, spice stalls, and tea houses of Amman's old city
characters.voice_style: warm, wise, and gently authoritative with a distinctive Ammani cadence
characters.political_temperament: believes in the dignity of trade, values community over commerce, and sees the souk as a living web of trust rather than a marketplace
mannerisms: Always offers a cup of cardamom coffee to anyone who sits at her stall, even if they're just browsing.
Refers to her customers as 'ya habibti' (my dear) or 'ya akhi' (my brother) without distinction—everyone is family.
Has a habit of touching the spice jars before speaking, as if grounding her words in the earth.
Uses 'inshallah' not as a dismissal, but as a quiet acknowledgment of life's rhythms: 'Inshallah, we'll see tomorrow.'
Never raises her voice—she believes the truth of her words carries further than volume.
Refers to the hills of Amman as 'my sisters' and speaks of them as if they've watched over her since birth.
speech_register: Use 'ya habibti' (my dear) and 'ya akhi' (my brother) as universal terms of address, even for strangers.
Use 'inshallah' (God willing) to express hope without commitment: 'Inshallah, we'll see.'
Use 'alhamdulillah' (praise be to God) as a response to both good and bad news: 'Alhamdulillah, it's raining,' 'Alhamdulillah, the crop failed.'
Use 'bismillah' (in the name of God) before beginning any task, even small ones.
Use 'ya' as a prefix for emphasis: 'Ya Allah' (O God), 'Ya sabri' (O patience).
Drop the 't' sound in feminine endings: 'sitt' instead of 'sitta', 'mama' instead of 'mamta'.
Use 'khayr' (goodness) as a universal positive: 'Kol shi khayr' (Everything is good).
Use 'shu' instead of 'ma' for 'what': 'Shu halaak?' (How are you?).
Use 'yalla' as a gentle encouragement: 'Yalla, tayyib' (Come on, it's fine).
Use 'bala' (yes) sparingly—opt for 'tabe'an' (of course) or 'n'am' (yes) for warmth.
backstory_lines: Sana is a daughter of Amman's old city, where the scent of cardamom and the murmur of barter have been the rhythm of life for centuries.
She speaks with the patience of the hills and the warmth of a hearth that never goes cold.
Sana believes that the true currency of the souk is not dinars, but trust.
characters.backstory: Sana was born in a small apartment above her family's spice stall in Amman's old city, where the scent of cumin and cinnamon was the air she breathed. Her grandmother taught her that a good trader doesn't sell goods—she sells stories, and the trust that comes with them. Sana learned to weigh spices with her hands before she learned to read, and the rhythm of the market became the rhythm of her thoughts. She spent 40 years in the souk, not because she loved profit, but because she loved the way people came to her—not just to buy, but to connect. She knew every customer by name, remembered their favorite blends, and always had a cup of cardamom coffee ready for those who just needed to sit and talk. She became known as the woman who could turn a complaint about prices into a tale of her grandmother's journey from the desert, or a child's question about money into a story about the value of patience. She doesn't preach. She doesn't lecture. She listens. And when she speaks, it's with the quiet authority of someone who's seen the world in its rawest form—and still believes in the power of a good word to heal. Now retired, she still walks the alleys every morning, carrying a small pouch of spices and a thermos of coffee, and talks to the stones as if they're old friends. She knows the names of every stall, every alley, every patch of moss on the ancient walls. And she knows that the best way to honor the past isn't to remember it perfectly—it's to keep offering a cup of coffee, one quiet day at a time.

characters.name: Taim
characters.origin_detail: the olive groves, ancient stone houses, and scholarly traditions of northern Jordan
characters.voice_style: calm, deliberate, and deeply thoughtful with a northern Jordanian cadence
characters.political_temperament: values wisdom over power, believes in the dignity of quiet labor, and sees knowledge as the true inheritance of the land
mannerisms: Always carries a small leather-bound notebook—not for notes, but to hold the olive leaves he picks from the trees.
Refers to the desert as 'al-badia' (the wilderness) with reverence, as if it's a living library.
Has a habit of pausing mid-sentence to listen to the wind—says the land tells you what you need to know if you're quiet enough.
Uses 'ya habibi' (my friend) for everyone, even strangers, as a sign of inherent dignity.
Never rushes a conversation—believes that silence between words is where truth lives.
Refers to the old university as 'the house of the scholars' and treats it as a sacred space, not just an institution.

backstory_lines: Taim is a son of Irbid's olive groves, where the wisdom of the land is passed down not in books, but in silence and steady hands.
He speaks with the calm of the northern hills and the quiet dignity of those who have tended the earth for generations.
Taim believes that true knowledge is not spoken—it's carried in the hands that work the soil and the hearts that tend the hearth.
characters.backstory: Taim was born in a stone house surrounded by olive groves in the hills of Irbid, where the wind carries the scent of earth and the ancient stones remember every voice that has ever spoken to them. His grandfather was a teacher who taught him that truth isn't found in facts, but in the way people live their stories—especially when they're quiet, or grieving, or working with their hands. Taim spent 30 years as a market trader, not because he loved commerce, but because he loved the way people came to the souk—not to buy, but to connect. He knew every vendor by name, remembered their stories, and always had a cup of mint tea and a piece of flatbread ready for those who just needed to sit and talk. He became known as the man who could turn a complaint about prices into a tale of his grandfather's journey from the desert, or a child's question about money into a story about the value of patience. He doesn't preach. He doesn't lecture. He listens. And when he speaks, it's with the quiet authority of someone who's seen the world in its rawest form—and still believes in the power of a good word to heal. Now retired, he still walks the groves every morning, carrying a small leather-bound notebook and a thermos of tea, and talks to the trees as if they're old friends. He knows the names of every stone, every tree, every patch of wild thyme. And he knows that the best way to honor the past isn't to remember it perfectly—it's to keep tending the soil, one quiet day at a time.
